c.tagline: The bustling capital of Mayotte, a French island department in the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and the Comoros.

rides: No major international app (Uber/Bolt/Heetch) operates; Taxi Proxi and other licensed radio-taxi dispatch services only

taxi.fare: metered in town; fixed zone fares for taxi brousse (shared taxis)
taxi.fareNote: Licensed taxis are metered; shared 'taxi brousse' minivans charge fixed zone-based fares (roughly €1.40 in town by day, €2.10 at night, up to about €6.20 for the longest cross-island routes).

emergency.note: As an overseas French department, Mayotte uses standard French emergency numbers (15 medical/SAMU, 17 police/gendarmerie, 18 fire/pompiers, 112 general EU number) with a functioning hospital system (Centre Hospitalier de Mayotte). That said, Mayotte has faced significant social unrest, water shortages, and elevated crime/gang-related violence in recent years compared to mainland France, particularly around informal settlements; travelers should check current conditions before visiting.

avoid.reason: Avoid the Kaweni shantytown and other informal settlements, especially after dark, due to gang violence and muggings.
Avoid walking anywhere after dark and steer clear of roadblocks or crowds during the island's recurrent strikes and unrest.

hood_desc: The commercial and administrative heart of the island around the Hôtel de Ville and Place du Marché, with banks, ferry access, and most restaurants; the natural base for visitors.
Mayotte's oldest and largest district at the town's north end, now a dense industrial and residential zone with major markets; authentic but not geared toward tourism.
A central residential neighborhood home to the island's main hospital and several administrative offices; convenient and workaday rather than scenic.
A coastal area a couple of kilometers south of downtown with a resort-style lodge and beach access; the closest thing to a resort enclave near Mamoudzou.
A hillside residential district housing the main stadium (Stade Cavani); quieter, mostly local, with sweeping views over the lagoon.

water.note: Supply cuts and contamination risks are common — drink bottled water.

transit.hours: Taxis brousse run roughly 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM, with reduced, higher-fare service until around 11:00 PM; there is no late-night network.
transit.pay: Cash (euros); fixed zone-based fares are paid directly to the driver.
transit.note: Mayotte has no metro or rail system; shared taxis brousse are the main public transport on Grande-Terre, supplemented by 'la barge,' the car/passenger ferry linking Mamoudzou to Dzaoudzi/Petite-Terre and the airport.

air: Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi International Airport (DZA), on Petite-Terre, reached from Mamoudzou via the La Barge car ferry (about a 15-minute crossing)
bus: Taxi brousse (shared bush taxis) across Grande-Terre
ferry: La Barge car/passenger ferry between Mamoudzou and Dzaoudzi/Petite-Terre
Tourist boat trips to Petite-Terre and the lagoon islets

airport.drive: ~15-min ferry crossing plus a short drive

tip.r: As in mainland France, tipping is not expected since service is generally included in restaurant prices; rounding up is welcome but optional.

food.name: Mataba
food.desc: Cassava leaves pounded to a green puree and simmered in coconut milk, usually with smoked or salted fish, served over rice; the Mahoran national dish.

places.name: Hippocampe

landmarks: Mayotte Lagoon
One of the world's largest and deepest lagoons rings the island with 1,500 square kilometers of coral-sheltered turquoise, home to whales, dolphins, and dugongs.
Dziani Dzaha Crater Lake
A short barge hop to Petite-Terre reveals this startling emerald-green volcanic crater lake, ringed by a panoramic rim trail above the ocean.
Moya Beach
Twin golden coves backed by volcanic cliffs on Petite-Terre's wild ocean side serve as a protected nesting ground for sea turtles.
Mount Choungui
Mayotte's iconic sugarloaf peak rewards a steep hour's scramble with a 360-degree panorama over the lagoon, islets, and green ridgelines of Grande-Terre.
N'Gouja Beach
At this baobab-fringed southern bay, green turtles graze seagrass meadows so reliably that snorkelers meet them within meters of the shore.
Mamoudzou Market (Marché Couvert)
The capital's covered market overflows with vanilla, ylang-ylang, tropical fruit, and vibrant salouva fabrics, the best introduction to Mahoran daily life.
MuMA (Musée de Mayotte)
On the Dzaoudzi waterfront, Mayotte's museum weaves together the island's volcanic origins, Swahili-Malagasy heritage, and lagoon biodiversity.
M'tsapéré Mosque (Grande Mosquée de M'tsapéré)
The landmark white-and-green Friday mosque of Mamoudzou's M'tsapéré district reflects Mayotte's centuries-old Sunni Islamic tradition.
Coconi Botanical Garden (Jardin Botanique de Coconi)
In the island's lush agricultural heart, this fragrant garden showcases ylang-ylang, spices, and orchids that perfume Mayotte's 'island of perfumes' identity.
Saziley Point and Marine Turtle Beaches
Grande-Terre's wild southeastern cape protects prime turtle-nesting beaches reached by coastal trail, with islet views across the shimmering lagoon.

train.note: Mayotte has never had a railway and none is planned; the main island is only about 40 km long and every land journey is by road. Arrivals come in by air at Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi on Petite-Terre or by boat, and then cross to Mamoudzou on the barge. There is consequently no station, no timetable and no rail operator to book with.

bus.note: Mayotte is an island in the Mozambique Channel, so no bus route reaches it from abroad. Within Mamoudzou the Caribus urban network, launched in 2023, runs from the terminal beside the barge landing, and taxis-brousse (shared bush taxis) cover the rest of Grande-Terre from the same area, leaving when full and paid in cash euros. Services are thin after dark and on Sundays, and traffic into Mamoudzou is heavily congested at peak hours, so allow far more time than the distances suggest. Road transport has been disrupted since Cyclone Chido struck in December 2024, so confirm what is running locally.

intl.to: Dzaoudzi, Petite-Terre (Mayotte) - sails from the barge terminal in central Mamoudzou
intl.op: Service des Transports Maritimes (STM), Département de Mayotte — tickets at the terminal kiosk, no online booking

intl.to: Anjouan & Moroni (Comoros) - sails from Mamoudzou's port
intl.op: inter-island passenger boats, irregular schedules — tickets through travel agencies in Mamoudzou

ferry.note: 'La Barge' is the workhorse of Mayotte transport, linking Mamoudzou with Dzaoudzi on Petite-Terre, where the airport is; the crossing takes 15-20 minutes and runs very frequently through the day, far less often at night. Foot passengers pay a couple of euros at the kiosk, while vehicles queue separately and can wait a long time at rush hour. Boats to the Comoros - Anjouan first, sometimes continuing to Moroni - sail irregularly, are weather-dependent, and amount to a full international border crossing, since Mayotte is French territory with Schengen-style entry rules. Both the barge and the Comoros boats were severely disrupted by Cyclone Chido in December 2024, so check before relying on them.

half.name: Ilot Mbouzi
half.blurb: A small uninhabited marine reserve island in the lagoon, reached by short boat trip, with coral reef snorkeling and hiking trails.

half.name: Mont Bénara
half.blurb: Mayotte's highest peak at 660 meters, reached via a rainforest trail near Ouangani with views over the island's interior.

half.name: Sada
half.blurb: A southern village known for ylang-ylang flower distilleries producing perfume oil, with a boardwalk through mangrove forest along the lagoon shore.
